title: That a man is soberly to judge of the divine ordinances
paragraphs: The proper field and subject of imposture is the unknown — in the first place because the strangeness itself lends it credit, and besides, by not being subject to our ordinary reasoning, it deprives us of the means of questioning and arguing it. For this reason, Plato says, it is much easier to satisfy an audience when speaking of the nature of the gods than of the nature of men, because the listeners' ignorance opens a fair, wide road and gives every liberty in the handling of obscure things. From this it comes that nothing is so firmly believed as what we know least about, and no people are so confident as those who entertain us with fables — your alchemists, your judicial astrologers, fortune-tellers, and physicians —
["All that sort of people." — Horace, Sat., i. 2, 2.]

To whom I would gladly add, if I dared, a pack of people who take upon themselves to interpret and supervise the designs of God himself, claiming to find the cause of every accident and to pry into the secrets of the divine will, in order to lay bare the incomprehensible motives of his works. And though the variety and the continual contradiction of events knock them from corner to corner, and toss them from east to west, they still keep up their futile inquisition, and with the same pencil paint both black and white.

Among one Indian nation there is a praiseworthy custom: when anything goes against them in some encounter or battle, they publicly ask pardon of the sun, who is their god, as though they had done some unjust act, always crediting their good or bad fortune to divine justice and submitting their own judgment and reason to it. It is enough for a Christian to believe that all things come from God, to receive them with acknowledgment of his divine and unsearchable wisdom, and so to accept them gratefully with whatever face they may wear. But I do not approve of the common practice of trying to confirm and support our religion by the success of our enterprises. Our belief has foundation enough without needing to be authorised by events. The people, accustomed to such plausible arguments, well-suited to their taste, are likely, when those arguments fail, to stagger in their faith too. So in this war we are now engaged in on account of religion, those who had the upper hand at the affair of Rochelabeille made loud boasts of it as an infallible approval of their cause, and then, when they had to excuse their misfortunes at Moncontour and Jarnac by calling them fatherly scourges and corrections — "because the people were not yet wholly at their mercy" — they show plainly enough what it is to draw two sorts of grist out of the same sack, and to blow hot and cold with the same mouth. It would be better to ground the common people in the solid, real foundations of truth. There was a fine naval battle won a few months ago under the command of Don John of Austria against the Turks; but it has also pleased God at other times to let us see victories just as great at our own expense. In short, it is a hard thing to reduce divine matters to our scales without losing a great deal of the weight in the spillage. And anyone who would try to give a reason why Arius and his Pope Leo, the principal heads of the Arian heresy, both died, at different times, of such similar and strange deaths (for, called away from disputation by a griping in the bowels, they both suddenly gave up the ghost on the privy), and would aggravate this divine vengeance by the circumstances of the place, might as well throw in the death of Heliogabalus, who was also killed in a privy. And Irenaeus, indeed, came to a similar end. God, pleased to show us that the good have something else to hope for, and the wicked something else to fear, than the fortunes or misfortunes of this world, manages and applies them according to his own hidden will and pleasure, and deprives us of the means of foolishly making a profit of them. So those people delude themselves who try to dive into these mysteries by the strength of human reason. They never strike one blow without taking two in return — of which St. Augustine makes a great proof against his opponents. It is a contest decided more by strength of memory than by force of reason. We must content ourselves with the light the sun is pleased to communicate to us by his rays; and whoever lifts up his eyes to take in more, let him not think it strange if, for the reward of his presumption, he loses his sight.
"Quis hominum potest scire consilium Dei? Aut quis poterit cogitare quid velit Dominus?"
["Who of men can know the counsel of God? or who can think what the will of the Lord is." — Book of Wisdom, ix. 13.]
